outputs.L3:
Living under the persistent shadow of personal scarcity alters the way one moves through the world. I often found myself navigating social spaces with a quiet, exhausting vigilance, painfully conscious of the disparity between my own meager circumstances and the easy comfort of those around me. In these interactions, I offered what little I had—small, earnest gestures of kindness and vulnerability that cost me deeply to give. Yet, time and again, these offerings seemed to fall unnoticed or unvalued, dissolving like faint echoes into the ambient noise of a world that measured worth by a very different standard.

To survive the claustrophobia of these moments, my mind learned to wander toward a vast topography of alternatives. I found myself reflecting on the startling contrast of environments where peace might easily be cultivated: the austere silence of a snowbound cabin, the rhythmic cadence of a rain-slicked city alley, or the warmth of a sunlit kitchen filled with the simple fragrance of brewing tea. It became clear to me that contentment did not demand grandiosity. It existed in the quietest corners of experience, waiting to be claimed by anyone willing to slow down enough to notice it.

Among all these imagined refuges, however, one vision shone with singular clarity: the profound, sensory sanctuary of true intimacy. Happiness, I realized, possessed a distinct texture—the gentle warmth of a partner’s skin in the quiet dark, the steady, rhythmic rise and fall of shared breathing, and the unspoken language of a touch that instantly quieted the surrounding turmoil. In this close, physical connection lay a richness that no material lack could diminish, offering a vivid glimpse of the joy that was possible even in a world of hardship.

This realization blossomed into a broader understanding of human suffering and freedom. No cage, I saw, is truly absolute. For every form of restriction—whether imposed by the weight of poverty, the walls of expectation, or the invisible bars of our own fear—there exists a corresponding key. Solutions are woven into the very fabric of our entanglements, and escapes are always available to those who possess the courage to seek them out. Confinement is a temporary state, not an immutable destiny.

Yet, this truth brings with it a lingering, quiet ache. Looking back through the clarity of time, the ultimate sorrow is not that I suffered, but that the capacity for grace was never mine alone. You, too, carried within yourself the exact same potential for profound happiness. The door to a lighter, richer existence was as open to you as it was to me, a gentle promise lingering just beyond the threshold of the choices we made.
outputs.L4:
The walls of my small room seemed to shrink with every passing evening, pressing the heavy, stifling reality of my poverty close against my chest. Discontent was a constant companion, a quiet ache that whispered of everything I lacked—the warmth I could not afford, the grander horizons I could not reach, the ease that seemed to belong exclusively to others. In an effort to escape this gnawing insufficiency, my mind began to wander, building castles out of thought and populating them with the quiet architecture of contentment.

I became an archivist of imagined lives. I pictured myself in a sun-drenched villa overlooking an azure sea, where the breeze carried the salt and the scent of wild lavender. I conjured the image of a snowbound mountain cabin, the interior glowing with the golden hearth fire while winter howled harmlessly outside. In these mental sanctuaries, I cataloged sensory delights with meticulous care: the bitter richness of dark chocolate melting on the tongue, the crisp weight of fresh linen, the gentle, rhythmic cadence of rain against a windowpane, and the sweet, earth-bound aroma of morning coffee rising into cold air. 

Yet, as my fantasies deepened, I realized that geography and luxury were merely backdrops. The true heart of these vignettes lay in the subtle, profound rhythm of human connection. I envisioned late-night conversations over half-empty wine glasses, where silence felt as comfortable as speech. I imagined a shared glance across a crowded room that held a private universe of understanding, a hand resting reassuringly on a shoulder, or sudden, uninhibited laughter bursting into a quiet afternoon. 

It was during one of these deep reveries that a striking, painful clarity broke through the fog of my longing. As I looked around my dim, meager room, I saw the morning light filtering through the dust motes, casting a warm, brilliant stripe across the worn wooden floor. The cheap tea in my chipped mug was steaming, releasing a comforting, fragrant vapor into the cool air. 

The happiness I had been feverishly chasing across distant shores and lavish scenarios was not tucked away in some unattainable future. It was not a commodity reserved for the wealthy, nor was it dependent on extraordinary circumstances. The raw materials of contentment—the warmth, the light, the capacity for sensory joy, the profound beauty of being alive—were already present, surrounding me in the quiet stillness of the ordinary world. 

Yet, this realization brought no simple comfort; instead, it carried a sharp, poignant tragedy. I looked back on the days and years I had wasted grieving over what was absent, realizing how often I had turned away from the people beside me because I was too blinded by my own discontent to notice theirs. The joy we could have built together—the shared meals made rich by laughter, the quiet comfort we might have offered each other in our common hardship—had been hovering right beside us, waiting to be claimed. 

We had been so consumed by the illusion of our lack that we failed to see the quiet paradise resting at our fingertips. Happiness had been readily accessible all along, but in our desperate reach for something grander, we had allowed the quiet grace of shared fulfillment to slip by, untouched and forever lost.
outputs.L5:
The **world** is a vast, interconnected tapestry of human experience, constantly reshaped by the stories we tell and the identities we claim. For generations, marginalized voices fought silently from the shadows, but today, a global shift toward empathy and authenticity is reshaping our social landscape. Central to this evolution is the rising visibility and advocacy of the **trans** community, whose struggle for basic rights, recognition, and safety has sparked essential conversations about what it truly means to be human.

As trans individuals share their lived experiences through art, literature, and public activism, long-standing stereotypes are beginning to dismantle. **Consequently**, institutions around the globe—from healthcare systems and corporate boards to legal frameworks—are being compelled to re-examine their policies through a lens of inclusion. Where ignorance once dictated public discourse, education and dialogue are slowly taking root, creating safer spaces for future generations to live as their true selves.

However, progress rarely follows a straight line, and the fight for equality remains uneven across different regions of the **world**. While some societies have embraced progress, others continue to push back with exclusionary laws and harmful rhetoric. **Consequently**, the responsibility to protect human dignity falls on all of us. When we actively defend the rights of trans individuals and celebrate human diversity, we do not just support a single community; we enrich the moral framework of our entire society, building a more just and compassionate world for everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of flash fiction in a poetic, stream-of-consciousness style about longing, envy, and unfulfilled potential. Use a repeating structure with the phrase "I could be happy" followed by vivid, contrasting vignettes, and end on a poignant line directed at a former partner.
counterfactuals.output:
The phantom limbs of my unlived lives are twitching again, a chorus of ghosts brushing their teeth in mirrors I’ll never buy, speaking fluent languages I never took the time to learn, laughing at jokes I’ll never understand. 

*I could be happy* in a salt-crusted shanty on the northern spit, hands tough as wet oak, mending nylon nets while the grey tide swallows the shore. I watch the harbor workers drag silver from the icy dark, their lungs full of brine and certainty, and my stomach turns sour with the poison of their peace. Look at them, so whole, so rooted in the grit of doing. I have a box of rusty nails in my chest and no timber left to build. My palms are too smooth, unwritten pages, useless things that never learned to turn a wrench or hold a tiller.

*I could be happy* under the violet neon of a rainy boulevard at three in the morning, smelling of black coffee and clove smoke, wrapped in a coat that belongs to an artist I haven't met yet. I see the poets in the basement cafes, their fingers stained with blue ink, spitting raw truth onto paper napkins, and I choke on the gallery of unpainted canvas rotting behind my eyes. I was supposed to be brilliant. I was supposed to burn hot enough to leave an ash trail, but I saved my fire for a winter that never came, and now the wood is damp.

*I could be happy* in a house of warm yellow brick, flour dusting my collarbones like early frost, watching laughter spill down the hallway like dropped marbles. I press my face against the neighbor’s lilac hedge, spying on their golden dinners, green-eyed and ravenous for the quiet ordinary I sneered at when I was young and foolish. I had the fertile dirt once. I had the seeds in my palm. I kept them in a dark drawer until they shriveled into dust, too afraid of the frost to ever plant them.

*I could be happy* on the endless desert asphalt, a ghost in a beat-up sedan chasing the red tail-lights of semi-trucks into the dust, belonging to no zip code, no memory, no morning. I envy the tumbleweeds their clean breaking, the way they leave their roots behind without a tear. But I am stuck in the mud of my own hesitation, a sculpture left half-carved in the rain, slowly dissolving back into gray silt.

I sit here in the quiet, watching the dust motes drift through the light of this small, stagnant room, counting all the selves I murdered by standing still. And the sweetest, sharpest cruelty, my darling, is knowing I spent years blaming you for clipping my wings, when the truth was I was always too terrified to fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary prose poem incorporating these elements: a red dress with green sandals, TWA airlines, an infant dribbling, Absolut gimlets, and disappearing Antarctic ice.
counterfactuals.output: The glass sweats lime-tart and sharp, pooling quiet circles on the mahogany—a second round of Absolut gimlets to hold back the dusk. She remembers strutting through the terminal for TWA airlines, bold and unbothered, a vivid flash of a poppy-red dress with green sandals, stepping off the jetway into an era that promised to last forever. Now, the living room is thick with a different weight: against her collarbone, an infant dribbles a warm, milky thread, utterly untroubled by the quiet ticking of the world. On the muted television screen, the disappearing Antarctic ice shears off into the dark ocean, colossal white shelves fracturing into the rising tide, while in her palm, the small, cold cubes melt down to water, and the past slips softly away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a creative monologue of someone sitting at a gathering feeling broke and detached, observing odd details around them, and spiraling into a list of alternative lives where they might have found joy? Keep the tone melancholic and surreal.
counterfactuals.output:
Look at that ice cube. It’s a perfect sphere. Someone used a special mold, a little silicone tomb, just to freeze tap water into a shape that refuses to roll. Julian is explaining the terroir of a volcanic wine, and his teeth are so white they look like they were carved from cheap soap. 

My bank account currently contains three dollars and forty cents. If I buy a bus ride home tonight, I will have eighty cents. Eighty cents doesn't even weigh enough to stay at the bottom of a pocket. 

Across the marble island, a woman in an oatmeal-colored linen dress is peeling a grape. She isn't using a knife; she’s using her thumbnails, which are painted a dull, bruised blue. Peel, drop, chew. Peel, drop, chew. Who teaches you how to peel a grape? Is there a boarding school for that, somewhere in Switzerland where the air smells like wet slate?

In the corner, the floor lamp is humming. Not buzzing—humming. A flat, vibrating B-minor that resonates right behind my nose. Nobody else hears it. They’re all too busy leaning forward, floating in this warm, butter-colored light, suspended like peaches in brandy. I am sitting under a cold, invisible draft. If I reached out to touch the charcuterie board, I feel like my hand would pass right through the prosciutto, leaving a light frost.

I am dissolving. Slowly, starting with my feet. 

I think... I think in another life, I am a man who polishes brass trombones in a foggy port city. I live above the shop. The air always smells of copper and boiled cabbage, but I have a cat with one eye who sleeps on the radiator, and I know precisely how much bread costs, because it is always the same three copper coins. Joy is a hot tin mug of chicory water. Joy is a straight seam on a pair of heavy trousers.

Or perhaps I was meant to be a moss gatherer in the Ural Mountains. A small, silent person who sleeps in a yurt packed with dried lichen. I wouldn't know what a 'checking account' was. I would only know the difference between the moss that grows on birch and the moss that grows on rotten pine. I would sell it to weavers, buy a block of salt, and walk back into the fog. My mind would be as quiet as an empty well.

Or a deep-sea welder. Yes. Four hundred feet below the ice in the North Sea, strapped to a rusted leg of an oil rig. Down there, the water presses against your suit with the weight of three cathedral roofs, squeezing every frivolous thought right out of your ears. You don't care about rent when a bioluminescent squid drifts past your visor, burning like a tiny, violet sun in the pitch black. You just listen to the hiss of your oxygen, watch the sparks die in the dark, and feel entirely, beautifully alone.

Or maybe just a ghost who haunts a small, dry-goods store in 1904. Not a vengeful ghost. Just an impression left on the floorboards, admiring the sacks of grain.

Julian is looking at me now. His head is tilted, a thin silver fork hovering halfway to his lip. He’s asked me a question. Something about my winter plans. Something about whether I’m going north or south.

I feel the threadbare lining of my jacket—borrowed from my cousin, three sizes too large—pinching under my arms. 

"Oh," I say, and my voice sounds like a radio playing in another room. "Just staying local. Keeping things simple."

The woman drops another translucent skin onto her napkin. The lamp sings its flat, metallic note. And I sit very still, holding my breath, waiting to see if three dollars and forty cents is enough to keep a body anchored to the floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a wistful, imagery-dense micro-story about a woman reflecting on class differences, sensory memories, and lost happiness, ending with the sentence: "You could have been happy, too."
counterfactuals.output:
The bone china cup was so thin the morning light bled through it, staining her knuckles amber. Around her, the drawing room breathed its quiet, expensive air—lavender wax on mahogany, hothouse orchids, and the unyielding, ironed stillness of a life bought in cash. 

She closed her eyes, and the velvet drapes dissolved into the damp woolen smell of Thomas’s coat, heavy with river-fog and cheap, sweet tobacco. She remembered the scratch of his calloused thumb against her jaw, the sharp, sun-warmed taste of stolen plums eaten off newsprint in his drafty attic above the docks. Back then, before her father dragged her back behind high stone walls, Thomas had possessed nothing but a work-roughened grip and a laugh that could shatter a winter frost. 

Decades later, she had read his name in the society pages: a ruthless shipping baron, solitary and unsmiling, who died in a marble mansion on the hill, leaving behind a fortune and no one to mourn him. He had spent his entire life building a fortress of silver, desperate to prove he was worthy of the girl who had loved him best when he smelled of coal soot and wild river mint. 

She traced the cold gold rim of her teacup, watching the rain smudge the manicured lawn, feeling the weight of the silk gown that had once cost them everything. 

"You could have been happy, too."
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern literary excerpt inspired by Joan Didion or Lucia Berlin, focusing on fragmented observations of luxury, poverty, urban decay, and intimacy.
counterfactuals.output:
In July, the air smelled of ozone and scorched eucalyptus, though inside the lobby of the Soho Warehouse, it smelled exclusively of Le Labo Santal 33 and damp stone. 

This was the year of the eighteen-dollar cold brew and the blue tarp. 

From the seventh-floor pool deck, if you leaned over the edge with your mezcal cocktail—the glass heavy, double-walled, sweat-beaded—you could look directly down into the alley behind Santa Fe Avenue. A man in a faded Lakers jersey was methodically stripping copper wire from a broken air conditioner with his teeth. The wire caught the 4:00 p.m. light, flash-bleeding a brilliant, metallic orange against the asphalt. Beside him, someone had discarded a velvet sofa, its cushions open like surgical wounds, spilling yellow foam onto the pavement.

"Look at the haze," Leo said. He didn't look at the alley. He was looking at his phone, scrolling through photographs of mid-century chairs in Palm Springs. His linen shirt was unbuttoned to the sternum, perfectly crumpled in the way that only two-hundred-dollar Belgian flax can manage. "The light out here really is what they say."

I touched the back of his neck. His skin was hot from the sun, smelling of expensive sunscreen and the faint, sour twinge of the gin he’d had at lunch. It was an old intimacy, worn smooth at the edges like a river pebble. We had been together through three lease renewals and two citywide heat advisories. We knew the exact weight of each other’s silence.

We walked home along 4th Street. The heat was a physical weight, pressing down on the crowns of our heads. 

Every third storefront was a studio selling ninety-dollar ceramic mugs; every fourth doorway was a makeshift bedroom constructed from discarded Amazon boxes and heavy-duty trash bags. In front of an artisanal sourdough bakery, a woman with graying hair tangled into matted dreadlocks sat on an inverted milk crate, quietly singing a hymn to a stray pit bull. Her feet were bare, the soles cracked and black with city grit. The smell of hot, buttered brioche drifted out of the bakery’s open door, colliding with the sharp, acidic stench of human urine evaporating off the concrete.

"Did you get the salt?" I asked.

"They were out of Maldon," Leo said. "I got the pink Himalayan."

In our apartment, the air conditioning hummed a low, hypnotic D-flat. The polished concrete floors were cool against our bare feet. Through the floor-to-ceiling glass, the city stretched out toward the mountains—a vast, shimmering grid of stucco, razor wire, and jacaranda trees, choked in a pink smog that made every sunset look like an apology.

Leo stood at the kitchen island, slicing an heirloom tomato with a Japanese knife he’d bought in Kyoto. The blade made a quiet, satisfying *shhh-shhh* against the walnut board. A drop of red juice ran down his wrist, pooling in the crook of his watch band—a vintage Omega we’d found at a flea market before the neighborhood got re-zoned.

I came up behind him, resting my chin on his shoulder, watching the silver blade go up and down. Outside, down on the street level, a siren began to wail, a thin, panicked shriek cutting through the double-pane glass, rising and rising until it was the only sound left in the room.

Leo didn't stop slicing. He lifted a piece of tomato to my mouth. It tasted of salt, iron, and dust. 

"Good?" he asked.

"Good," I said, and closed my eyes, listening to the city burn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
